explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. Ahaz, king of Judah, “…walked in the ways of the kings of Israel…” instead of doing what was right in the LORD's eyes. Remember he comes from David's line, so he's wandering a long way from the family recipe. The text names Israel's kings and nobody else.

Moab never comes up in this verse, friend. The text says Ahaz “…walked in the ways of the kings of Israel…” and that's the only crowd it names. It's an easy one to grab when you're guessing at a list of kings. Next time, let the verse do the picking.

Egypt is a big name, so I get the pull. But verse 3 doesn't mention it. It says Ahaz “…walked in the ways of the kings of Israel…” and that's who he follows instead of the LORD. Same road, different crowd than you picked.

Not quite, friend. Verse 4 says Ahaz sacrificed and burned incense “…on the high places, on the hills, and under every green tree.” The verse never names the temple at all. This man had more spots than I have cookie cutters, and I used to have six.
Right, baker. The text says Ahaz “…sacrificed and burned incense on the high places, on the hills, and under every green tree.” Those are the places the verse names. The temple isn't one of them.

Yes, baker. Verse 7 says Ahaz sent messengers to Tiglath-pileser, king of Assyria. Judah's king is under attack, and Assyria is who he calls. I'd have phoned a different number, but that's the call he made.

Egypt's a fair guess, but not this time. So, a king of Egypt, shows up later in 2 Kings 17:4, in a different story. Here in verse 7, Ahaz sends his messengers to Tiglath-pileser, king of Assyria. Keep the two stories in separate boxes.

Hiram, king of Tyre, sends his servants to Solomon in 1 Kings 5:1, which is a different story. In this one, Ahaz sends his messengers to Tiglath-pileser, king of Assyria. Different king, right idea, since Ahaz really is asking another king for help.

That's what he says, baker. Ahaz tells the king of Assyria, “I am your servant and your son.” Then he asks him to come up and save him from the kings of Aram and Israel. A king calling himself somebody else's servant is a lot to say in one sentence.

Ally and equal would sound sturdy, but that's not what Ahaz writes. He says, “I am your servant and your son.” Nothing in his message puts him on the same level as Assyria's king. He's asking to be saved, and he words it that way.

It's a friendly guess, but Ahaz doesn't go with friendly. His words are “I am your servant and your son.” Then he asks Tiglath-pileser, king of Assyria, to come up and save him. Not a casual note to a neighbor.

explanations.answer: Silver and gold from the LORD's house and the palace
explanations.explanation: You've got it, friend. Ahaz took the silver and gold found in the house of the LORD and in the treasuries of the king's palace. Then he sent it as a gift to the king of Assyria. Silver and gold from two places, all in one gift.

explanations.answer: Horses and chariots from the royal stables
explanations.explanation: Horses and chariots? Ooh, fancy, friend, but that's not the list. Verse 8 says Ahaz took silver and gold from the house of the LORD and from the treasuries of the king's palace, and that's what he sent to the king of Assyria. I'd love to see a chariot in a gift box, though. I'd need a bigger box than any cookie box I've got.

explanations.answer: Bronze and iron from the city armories
explanations.explanation: Bronze and iron would be a heavy delivery, but that's not the list. The gift is silver and gold, taken from the house of the LORD and the treasuries of the king's palace. He sent it to the king of Assyria. The armories aren't mentioned.
Yes, baker. The king of Assyria marched up to Damascus and captured it. He also put Rezin, king of Aram, to death. Rezin was one of the two kings who came against Ahaz, so that's a big turn.

This one's actually true, friend. Verse 9 says the king of Assyria marched up to Damascus and captured it. He also put Rezin, king of Aram, to death. Rezin had come against Jerusalem, so Ahaz's call got an answer.
Not this time, baker. Verse 9 says the king of Assyria took the people of Damascus to Kir as captives. They were not left in their city. Their city was captured and its people were carried off.
Right, baker. The king of Assyria took the people of Damascus to Kir as captives. They didn't get to stay in their city. It's a hard part of the story, and the text doesn't soften it.

explanations.answer: Builds the altar by Ahaz's instructions
explanations.explanation: That's what happens, friend. Uriah the priest builds the altar according to all the instructions King Ahaz sent from Damascus. He doesn't change a thing, as far as the text tells us. I once had a recipe card that I followed less closely than that.

explanations.answer: Sends the plans back to Damascus
explanations.explanation: Nothing in the text says Uriah returns the plans, baker. Verse 11 says he built the altar according to all the instructions King Ahaz had sent. That's what he does with them in this verse.

explanations.answer: Locks the plans away in the temple
explanations.explanation: Locking plans away isn't what verse 11 tells us, baker. Uriah the priest builds the altar according to all the instructions King Ahaz sent from Damascus. The verse says he built it, and it doesn't mention any locking away.

Right, baker. Verse 11 says Uriah completed the altar before King Ahaz returned. So when the king gets back, the altar is already finished. The text puts the finish line before the king's return, and that's all it says about timing.
It's actually true, friend. Uriah the priest completed the altar before King Ahaz returned from Damascus. Verse 11 says so plainly. So the king comes home to a finished altar.

explanations.answer: Approaches it and presents offerings on it
explanations.explanation: You've got it. When the king came back from Damascus and saw the altar, he approached it and presented offerings on it (verse 12). Verse 13 then lists what he offered, starting with his burnt offering and his grain offering.

explanations.answer: Has it torn down and carried away
explanations.explanation: Ahaz is the one who sent the plans for this altar, baker, so tearing it down doesn't fit. Verse 12 says he approached it and presented offerings on it. That's what the king does with it.

explanations.answer: Orders Uriah to move it outside the city
explanations.explanation: Not this one, friend. Verse 12 says the king saw the altar, approached it and presented offerings on it. Moving it outside the city isn't mentioned. The moving comes later, in verse 14, and it's the bronze altar that Ahaz moves.

explanations.answer: Moves it to the north side of the new altar
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. Ahaz took the bronze altar that stood before the LORD and put it on the north side of the new altar. It had been standing between the new altar and the house of the LORD. So the bronze altar ends up on the north side of the new one.

explanations.answer: Sends it off to the king of Assyria
explanations.explanation: Ahaz does send a gift to Assyria earlier, but it's silver and gold (verse 8). The bronze altar doesn't go anywhere near Assyria. Verse 14 says he put it on the north side of the new altar. It just gets shoved over.

explanations.answer: Breaks it apart and melts down the bronze
explanations.explanation: No melting in this verse, friend. Ahaz took the bronze altar and put it on the north side of the new altar. It's moved, not broken up. In the next verse he even says he'll use it to seek guidance.

Yes, baker. Ahaz tells Uriah to offer the morning burnt offering, the evening grain offering and all the people's offerings on the great altar. He keeps the bronze altar for himself, to seek guidance. Uriah gets the daily work, and the king keeps the bronze altar for himself.

Bethel isn't in this story, friend. Ahaz says to offer on “…the great altar…” and that's the new one Uriah built. The bronze altar he saves for seeking guidance. So all of it happens right there in Jerusalem.

explanations.answer: The altars on the high places
explanations.explanation: Ahaz does offer on the high places back in verse 4, so it's a fair thought. But here his command to Uriah is to offer on the great altar. That's the new one in Jerusalem. The bronze altar is for him to seek guidance.
The text shows no pushback, baker. Verse 16 says, “So Uriah the priest did just as King Ahaz had commanded.” That's all the verse tells us about his response.
Right, friend. Verse 16 says, “So Uriah the priest did just as King Ahaz had commanded.” There's no objection recorded anywhere. The text moves straight from the king's orders to Uriah doing them.
Yes, baker. Ahaz cut off the frames of the movable stands and removed the bronze basin from each of them. The text says it plainly. He's not tinkering, he's taking things apart.
This one's true, friend. Verse 17 says King Ahaz cut off the frames of the movable stands and removed the bronze basin from each of them. Then he went on to the Sea in the same verse.

That's right, baker. Verse 18 says Ahaz removed the Sabbath canopy and closed the royal entryway on account of the king of Assyria. That's the same king he sent silver and gold to earlier. The text gives the king of Assyria as the reason, and doesn't say more than that.

Egypt never shows up in this chapter, friend. Verse 18 says Ahaz did these things on account of the king of Assyria. That's the king he'd already sent silver and gold to. Keep Assyria in your head for this whole chapter.

Babylon, huh? Nice try, baker, but it never shows up in this chapter. The text says Ahaz removed the Sabbath canopy and closed the royal entryway on account of the king of Assyria. Assyria is who he'd been dealing with since verse 7. That king's name is all over this chapter, like flour on my apron.

That's him, baker. Ahaz is buried with his fathers in the City of David, and his son Hezekiah reigns in his place. A new king takes the throne. This chapter leaves it right there, so the story isn't over.

Manasseh does become king, but later. According to 2 Kings 20:21, he's the son of Hezekiah, so he comes after the king who follows Ahaz. The son who reigns in Ahaz's place is Hezekiah. Right family, one generation too far.

Josiah did become king, friend. 2 Kings 22:1 says he was eight years old when he became king. The son who takes over from Ahaz, though, is Hezekiah. Good name, just not the one for this spot in the lineup.
